scams.name: DFW & Love Field Unlicensed Airport Taxi Scam
scams.tldr: Unlicensed drivers intercept arriving tourists outside baggage claim, offer a "cheaper" or "faster" ride, then charge three to six times the metered fare at the destination.
scams.description: Unlicensed drivers intercept arriving tourists outside baggage claim, offer a "cheaper" or "faster" ride, then charge three to six times the metered fare once you reach your destination.
scams.avoidance: Use the official yellow-taxi queue curbside at the terminal's lower level, where flat zone rates to downtown are posted. Order Uber or Lyft from the app and walk to the designated pickup zone at your terminal's signed gate. Take the DART Orange Line from DFW Airport to downtown Dallas for $3.00 one-way in about 50 minutes. Photograph the license plate and the dashboard permit before loading any luggage. If you are overcharged, call DFW Airport Police at 972-973-3210 before paying and file a formal complaint.
scams.location: Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport Terminals A, B, C, D, E arrivals curbs, DFW Skylink train stations, Dallas Love Field baggage-claim exits, Terminal 2 curbside rideshare zones, DART Orange Line DFW Airport Station

scams.name: 'Ran Out of Gas' Fake Jewelry Roadside Distraction Scam
scams.tldr: A stranger claims to have run out of gas and offers fake gold jewelry as collateral for cash. Travelers report it is still running across North Dallas.
scams.description: A stranger flags you down claiming to have run out of gas, then offers gold-looking jewelry, watches, or other valuables as collateral or payment in exchange for cash. The jewelry is worthless, and travelers report that the scheme is still running across North Dallas.
scams.avoidance: Decline every roadside "ran out of gas" approach at Dallas gas stations, tollway exits, and parking lots. Never accept gold-looking jewelry, watches, or valuables from a stranger as collateral or payment under any circumstances. If the stranger persists, physically leave the area: get in your car and drive to a staffed location or the nearest police station. Refuse to drive a stranger to an ATM, a "nearby" gas station, or any second location for any reason. Report the encounter to the Dallas Police non-emergency line at 214-744-4444 with the intersection and a physical description.
scams.location: Dallas North Tollway service-road exits, Central Expressway (US-75) northbound ramps, Lemmon Avenue near Dallas Love Field, Preston Road commercial strip, Inwood Road gas stations

scams.name: Downtown Dallas Aggressive Panhandling & Phone-Access Scams
scams.tldr: This scam evolved between 2024 and 2025 from passive signs at freeway exits into active approach scams on pedestrian corridors.
scams.description: This scam evolved between 2024 and 2025 from passive signs at freeway exits into active approach scams on pedestrian corridors. Organized groups work specific intersections on shift patterns, and travelers note that they can be hard to distinguish from genuinely homeless people. The approach often turns into a request to borrow your phone, which the scammer then grabs and runs off with.
scams.avoidance: Never hand an unlocked phone to a stranger; if they need to make a call, dial it yourself on speaker while keeping the phone in your hand. Say "No" firmly and keep walking without breaking stride, because engaging in conversation is the scammer's first win. Keep valuables and wallets in front pockets or zipped bags, not in back pockets, when walking through Deep Ellum or the West End at night. If you are followed or touched, step into any staffed business, hotel lobby, or 7-Eleven and ask the clerk to call 911. Report aggressive or threatening approaches to the Dallas Police non-emergency line at 214-744-4444 with the intersection and time.
scams.location: Downtown Dallas West End, Deep Ellum entertainment strip, Uptown McKinney Avenue, Bishop Arts District, highway-ramp medians along I-30 and I-35E, Klyde Warren Park perimeter

scams.name: Dallas Concert Ticket Resale & Fake Promoter Fraud
scams.tldr: On February 25, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that a Dallas man had been sentenced to 75 months in federal prison for a $1.1 million concert-promotion fraud, after posing as a licensed promoter for artists including Bad Bunny and Beyoncé.
scams.description: On February 25, 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice announced that a Dallas man had been sentenced to 75 months in federal prison for a $1.1 million concert-promotion fraud, after posing as a licensed promoter for artists including Bad Bunny and Beyoncé. WFAA and the Dallas Morning News both covered the sentencing, which underscored a pattern that continues at Dallas venues through 2026.
scams.avoidance: Buy only from official primary sellers (Ticketmaster, AXS, or the venue box office) or from verified secondary platforms that offer buyer protection. Refuse every Zelle, Cash App, or Venmo payment request for tickets; legitimate resellers never ask for payment off-platform. Pay by credit card so that a chargeback dispute is possible if the ticket fails to scan at the venue gate. Verify the seller's profile age, mutual-friend count, and review history before sending any money on Facebook Marketplace. If you are scammed, file a Dallas Police report at 214-744-4444 within 24 hours and dispute the charge with your bank or card issuer.
scams.location: American Airlines Center concourse approaches, Dos Equis Pavilion Fair Park, The Factory in Deep Ellum entry lines, Toyota Music Factory in Irving, Facebook Marketplace and Craigslist Dallas listings
